title: Discussions that Promote Societal Belonging
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Written days after the Sandy Hook shooting, this short piece argues that a public tragedy, handled carefully, can help students find a place in society rather than simply being material for fixation. Stuart begins by stating his discomfort: he would rather simply endorse Jim Burke's call to carry on the ordinary work of teaching, and he condemns the opportunism that follows every disaster. He then names his goal, 'societal belonging': a student's sense of belonging to society and having a part in its flourishing. His method is structured. Freshmen closely read articles presenting different viewpoints, framed by the teacher with explicit vocabulary instruction and support for a written response. They then write reflectively, sometimes using Graff's argument template, before a discussion scaffolded with They Say / I Say sentence templates. His claim is that this reading-writing-discussion sequence makes room for emotion while producing the thoughtful civic talk that belonging depends on.
points: Stuart defines 'societal belonging' as a student's sense of membership in society and of having a part in promoting its flourishing, and treats it as an instructional aim.
He draws a line between opportunistic fixation on tragedy and deliberate classroom use of it, placing his strategy on the side of ordinary, careful teaching.
The sequence is deliberate: framed article-of-the-week reading with explicit vocabulary, then reflective writing, then discussion, so students talk only after they have read closely and written.
Graff's Clueless in Academe template and Graff and Birkenstein's They Say / I Say discussion templates are the scaffolds that turn emotional reactions into clear, collegial exchange.
quotes: A big part of me hates writing this post, instead wanting simply to admire and affirm Jim Burke's noble call to continue the promotion of human flourishing that teachers work at each day, to conduct the normal business that is our calling. I love this sentiment because it flies in the face of the opportunism that rears its head during every tragedy, whether it be in the form of East Coast stores profiteering from Hurricane Sandy or reporters eagerly interviewing children mere hours after the Sandy Hook shootings.

Yet, despite abhorring that ugly human desire to fixate on tragedy, I also feel that moments like this can help us develop students who flourish. Mass shootings, even in their expression of purest evil, can promote discussions that help our students find a place in society.

To promote the close reading, I create article-of-the-week style documents and I do the simple work of framing them, of explicitly teaching key vocabulary words, and of giving them some structure to help with composing a written response. In the wake of last Friday's events, I gave them one article that I felt reflected the complexities and the widely felt urgency of gun control.

Once they've written, it's time either that day or the next for some discussion. Again, I like using templates to help students express their thoughts in thoughtful and clear ways (They Say, I Say, by Graff and Birkenstein, is the king of discussion templates).

The simple acts of closely reading and responding to several viewpoints on an issue promotes beautiful, society-strengthening discussion. It allows for emotion, but it also promotes the kind of thoughtful discussion that societal belonging depends upon.
